blocks.title: Spreadsheet
blocks.md: A **spreadsheet** is a program that arranges data in **rows** (numbers 1, 2, 3...) and **columns** (letters A, B, C...). Each box is a **cell**. B3 means column B, row 3. A spreadsheet can calculate automatically.

blocks.title: Formulas
blocks.md: Start a formula with **=**. Examples: =A1+A2, =B2\*C2, =SUM(B2:B5) (adds B2 to B5), =AVERAGE(B2:B5). Press Enter. If you change a number, the answer changes by itself. Use + - \* / for add, subtract, multiply, divide.

blocks.caption: A spreadsheet table with three fruits, kilograms sold and price per kilogram.
blocks.alt: Table: mango 10 kg at 500, pineapple 6 kg at 700, banana 8 kg at 300.

blocks.title: Charts
blocks.md: A **bar chart** compares amounts. A **line chart** shows change over time. A **pie chart** shows parts of a total. Always give a chart a title and label the axes.

blocks.title: Mistakes
blocks.md:
- No = sign: the cell shows text instead of a result.
- Typing the answer by hand: it will not update.
- Writing the cell reference as 3B instead of B3.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: In the sheet above, write a formula for the income from mango (kg in B2, price in C2) and compute it.
steps: Income = kg x price, so D2 = B2\*C2.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Total kilograms sold: B2=10, B3=6, B4=8. Write the formula and compute it.

blocks.title: Internet and web
blocks.md: The **Internet** is a worldwide network of computers. The **World Wide Web** is the pages you view on it. A **browser** shows web pages. A **search engine** finds pages for words you type. A **website address** (URL) is like www.example.com.

blocks.title: Searching well
blocks.md: Use clear key words, e.g. 'rainfall Douala'. Check who made the page. Compare two sources. Not everything online is true. Copying a text word for word without saying where it came from is not honest.

blocks.caption: An email with the To box, Subject box, message area and Send button.
blocks.alt: Email window with To, Subject, message text and Send.

blocks.title: Email
blocks.md: An **email address** looks like name@example.com. To send: click New message, type the address in **To**, a **Subject**, the message, and click Send. You can add an **attachment**. **Reply** answers a message. **Inbox** holds received mail.

blocks.title: Safety
blocks.md:
- Never share your password.
- Do not open attachments from people you do not know.
- Do not give personal details to strangers.
- A message promising a prize may be a trick (phishing).

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Why is 'prize@free-win.example' in an unknown email a warning sign?
steps: It offers something for nothing from an unknown sender.
Prize messages often ask for personal data: a phishing sign.
blocks.answer: Do not open or reply; delete it.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: List the steps to email a homework file to your teacher.
steps: Open your email, click New message, type the teacher's address and a subject.
Click Attach, choose the file, then Send.
blocks.answer: New message, address, subject, attach, send

blocks.title: Slides
blocks.md: A **presentation program** lets you make a series of **slides** to show an audience. Each slide can have a title, short text, pictures, charts and sound. You can add **transitions** between slides and **animations** to objects.

blocks.title: Good design
blocks.md:
- One main idea per slide.
- Short points, not long sentences (about 6 lines at most).
- Large text (at least 24 points) in a clear font.
- Strong contrast between text and background.
- Use pictures that help, not decorate.

blocks.caption: A slide with a title and three short bullet points.
blocks.alt: Slide with a title bar and three short bullet points.

blocks.title: Making a presentation
blocks.md: Choose a layout (Title slide, Title and content). Click to add the title and text. Use Insert to add a picture or table. Use **Slide Show** to run it. Practise what you will say. Do not read every word from the slide.

blocks.title: Mistakes
blocks.md:
- Too much text on a slide.
- Dark text on a dark background.
- Too many animations, which distract the audience.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: A slide has 12 long sentences. How would you improve it?
steps: Too much text; split it across several slides.
Keep three to five short bullets per slide and enlarge the text.
blocks.answer: Split the slide and shorten the text.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Choose the better colour pair for a projector: yellow text on white or dark blue text on white.
steps: Contrast matters: yellow on white is hard to read.
Dark blue on white gives strong contrast.

blocks.title: Tables
blocks.md: A **table** has rows and columns of cells. Use Insert then Table and choose the number of rows and columns. Tables are good for timetables, price lists and class lists. You can add or delete rows and columns, merge cells and add borders.

blocks.title: Pictures and layout
blocks.md: Use Insert then Picture to add an image. Drag a corner handle to resize it **without distortion**. **Text wrapping** decides how the text flows around the picture. **Margins** are the empty spaces at the page edges. **Orientation** can be portrait (tall) or landscape (wide).

blocks.caption: A table with times and subjects for Monday and Tuesday.
blocks.alt: Timetable table with columns for time, Monday and Tuesday.

blocks.title: Headers, footers and tools
blocks.md: A **header** is text at the top of every page; a **footer** is at the bottom. Page numbers are often placed in the footer. **Find and Replace** changes every copy of a word at once. **Spell check** underlines possible mistakes; always read your text yourself too.

blocks.title: Mistakes
blocks.md:
- Pulling a side handle of a picture stretches it; use a corner handle.
- Very large pictures make the file big.
- Do not use spaces to line up columns; use a table or tab stops.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: How many cells are in a table with 5 rows and 4 columns?

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: A school name appears 12 times as 'GBHS' but must be 'GBPHS'. What tool changes all at once?
steps: Find: GBHS. Replace with: GBPHS. Choose Replace All.

lessons.title: Binary numbers: the basics
lessons.programRef: Cameroon secondary (general education) Computer Studies / ICT programme, Form 2 — to be checked against the official programme
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Convert small binary numbers to denary and back
Know bit, byte and the storage units
reviewNotes: 1024 vs 1000 convention to be agreed with the teacher.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Binary
blocks.md: Computers use **binary**: only the digits 0 and 1. A **bit** is one binary digit. **8 bits make 1 byte**. Binary matches the two states of electronic switches: off (0) and on (1).

blocks.title: Place values
blocks.md: Binary place values double from the right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. To convert binary to **denary** (ordinary numbers), add the place values where there is a 1. Example: 1011 = 8 + 2 + 1 = 11.

blocks.caption: Four boxes with place values 8, 4, 2, 1 and the bits 1101.
blocks.alt: Row of boxes 8, 4, 2, 1 with bits 1, 1, 0, 1 under them.

blocks.title: Denary to binary
blocks.md: Find the largest place value that fits, write 1 there and subtract. Continue to the right. Example: 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, so 13 = 1101 (place 2 is 0).

blocks.title: Storage units
blocks.md: 1 byte = 8 bits. 1 KB (kilobyte) = 1024 bytes, 1 MB = 1024 KB, 1 GB = 1024 MB (the usual school convention).
